An Obesity Trend Quest Walkthrough!

obesity-trend-quest.Rmd

Welcome! What can this package do?

Obesity Trend Quest lets you explore how adult obesity estimates have changed across countries and continents. You can use the interactive app, or work with the packaged data and comparison function in R.

It’s designed for students, public-health analysts, and curious readers. Use it to spot and discuss patterns, but not to decide why a trend happened or whether a policy worked.

Install and open the app

First time using Obesity Trend Quest? You’ll need an internet connection to install it from GitHub. Run these commands in your R Console. You only need to install the package once; if you already have it, skip this step.

options(repos = c(CRAN = "https://cloud.r-project.org"))
install.packages("remotes")
remotes::install_github(
  "ETC5523-2026/etc5523-assignment-4-shro-ots"
)

Once installation finishes, open the app by running this command in your R Console:

obstrendquest::run_app()

Pick a path to explore

The app gives you three ways to compare estimates:

  • One country vs. the rest of its continent: see how a country or area compares with the average for the other included places in its continent.
  • Compare countries/areas: choose 2–5 places and see how their estimates change over time.
  • Compare continents: compare estimates averaged across 2–5 continents.

Choose the places you’re interested in, then set the year range. The graph updates to show the trends, and the quick-read summary gives you a handy snapshot of how each estimate changed between the first and last years you chose.

Making sense of the numbers

The lines show estimated percentages of adults over time. The summary shows the starting estimate, the ending estimate, and the difference in percentage points.

For example, a change from 10% to 14% is an increase of 4 percentage points and not a 4% relative increase. If the difference is positive, the estimate went up and if it’s negative, it went down.

A few limitations to keep in mind

These figures are estimates, not a count of people. The app can help you spot patterns, but it can’t tell you what caused them or whether a policy worked. Continent comparisons give every included country or area equal weight, regardless of population, so they aren’t estimates for the average person in that continent.
